client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed with sadness since my grandmother passed away. It’s hard to focus at work, and I keep catching myself zoning out or just feeling like I’m going through the motions. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like it’s just something I have to get through on my own.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss right now, and that sadness is making everyday tasks feel especially difficult. While you're wondering if you have to go through this alone, I hear how much this pain is affecting you—your voice sounds heavy with it. Would it be okay to explore what "getting through it on your own" looks like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Getting through it on my own feels like I’m just supposed to push through the sadness and pretend I’m fine, even though I’m not. I don’t know if I believe that talking about it will really change anything—it just feels like I’m stuck in this cycle of feeling bad and then feeling guilty for not handling it better.
therapist: I hear how exhausting it feels to wear that mask of "being fine" while carrying so much grief inside. The way your voice tightens when you talk about guilt makes me wonder if part of you believes you *should* be handling this differently—would you say that pressure comes from somewhere specific?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the pressure comes from... well, I guess it’s partly from my family. They expect me to be strong because I’ve always been the “together” one. But also, I put it on myself—like I should be able to just move on or figure it out. It’s frustrating because I don’t even know what “handling it differently” would look like. I feel stuck between pretending I’m okay and not knowing how to actually *be* okay.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful expectations—your family's view of you as the strong one, and your own belief that grief should follow a certain timeline. The way your voice rises when you talk about this makes me think this frustration runs deep. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to grieve without any "shoulds" attached to it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... the idea of letting go of the "shoulds" makes me anxious. If I'm not the strong one, who am I? My whole family leans on me. And part of me feels like if I stop pushing through the grief, I'll just collapse completely. 

It's like there's a voice in my head saying "You've held it together this long, why can't you just keep going?" But at the same time, I'm so tired.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying not just grief, but also the weight of being the person everyone relies on—and that’s a lot. The way your voice speeds up when you talk about collapsing makes me wonder if part of you fears that letting go of this role might feel like losing yourself. What would it feel like to imagine a middle ground—where you could still be there for your family, but also allow yourself the space to grieve?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I do feel like I’m the glue holding everything together, and the thought of stepping back even a little makes me panic. What if everything falls apart? I’ve always been the one everyone turns to, and I don’t even know who I’d be if I wasn’t that person. The idea of a middle ground sounds nice, but it also feels impossible—like I’d be letting everyone down if I tried.
therapist: It sounds like this role of being the "glue" has become such a core part of how you see yourself that the idea of shifting it feels almost threatening. Your voice has an urgent quality when you talk about this—like you're holding up something very heavy. What do you think might happen if, just for small moments, you let yourself *not* be the one holding everything together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know...the thought of stepping back even for small moments makes me feel really guilty. What if someone needs me and I'm not there? I keep imagining things falling apart because I wasn't holding them together. 

But at the same time, I'm so exhausted all the time. It's like I'm running on empty but can't stop because the alternative seems worse.
therapist: I hear how deeply torn you feel—the exhaustion is palpable in your voice, yet the fear of what might happen if you pause feels equally real. That guilt seems to be keeping you locked in this exhausting cycle. What do you imagine would be the very first, smallest sign that things *wouldn't* fall apart without you holding them together constantly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know... even thinking about letting go a little bit makes my chest feel tight. Maybe if the dishes piled up for one night? But then I imagine my roommate noticing and thinking I'm lazy. It's not even about the dishes really, it's about proving I'm not a disappointment.
therapist: It sounds like even small steps toward self-care feel loaded with meaning—like the dishes aren’t just dishes, but proof of your worth. That tightness in your chest tells me how high the stakes feel. What do you think it would take for you to see yourself as someone who *deserves* rest, rather than someone who has to earn it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don’t know... it feels impossible to think of myself as deserving rest. Every time I try to relax, I just feel guilty, like I’m wasting time or being lazy. Even when I do take breaks, I can’t enjoy them because I’m thinking about all the things I *should* be doing instead. It’s like I’m wired to always be productive, and if I’m not, I’m failing somehow.
therapist: It sounds like rest feels almost like a betrayal of the standards you’ve set for yourself—and that guilt follows you even when you try to pause. Your voice has a tense quality when you talk about this, like you’re stuck in a cycle of proving your worth through productivity. What would it feel like to imagine that rest isn’t a failure, but something that might actually help you show up more fully for the things that matter to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It’s hard to imagine rest as anything but failure because I feel like I’m wasting time when I’m not doing something productive. Even when I try to rest, I can’t fully relax because I’m constantly thinking about what I *should* be doing instead. It’s like I’m always behind, and taking a break just makes it worse.
therapist: It sounds like rest has become tangled up with guilt for you—like pressing pause means falling further behind. The way your voice tightens when you talk about "wasting time" makes me wonder if this belief has been with you for a long time. What do you think might shift if you could see rest as part of being productive, rather than the opposite of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I’ve always felt like rest is a luxury I can’t afford—like every moment I’m not working, I’m failing somehow. Even when I try to relax, my mind races with all the things I *should* be doing. I’m not sure how to shift that mindset, though. It feels like if I start seeing rest as productive, I’ll just end up slacking off and falling even further behind.
therapist: It sounds like rest feels like a slippery slope—like if you give yourself an inch, you'll lose all control. That fear of "falling behind" seems to keep you locked in this exhausting cycle. What would it feel like to experiment with just five minutes of intentional rest, where you remind yourself that pausing might actually help you move forward with more clarity?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
